processing: A green tea, fixed and dried without oxidation; producers describe a newer style of processing, but the details are not published.
harvest_season: Spring, as is usual for the famous green teas of Hubei.
taste_profile: A clean, lasting fresh fragrance over a light green-tea body; no fuller tasting detail is well established.

brewing.notes: Three grams is the usual measure. Treat it as any Chinese spring green: water well off the boil, and do not let the leaf sit in the pot between steeps.

vintage_note: Sold the usual way for a Chinese green tea: current year's spring harvest, drunk within about a year. Look for a stated picking date. It has no ageing tradition.
description:
Longzhong Cha is a green tea from Longzhong, west of the old city of Xiangyang in northern Hubei. The place is the draw: it is known as the retreat of Zhuge Liang, the Three Kingdoms strategist, and the tea is sold partly to the people who come to see his sites.

Little has been published about how it is made beyond the general outline of a green tea and a mention of newer processing methods. The finished leaf is described as silvery grey, which sets it apart from the deep green strands of many Hubei teas.

The cup should be bright green and clear, with a fresh aroma that holds on through the steep. Brew it with cooler water and short infusions, as with other spring greens, since heat is the quickest way to lose that aroma.

Local promotion calls it one of Hubei's top teas, but such rankings are marketing more than measurement. When buying, ask for the current spring's tea and check that the leaf smells fresh rather than flat.
history: Little is documented about when Longzhong tea began or who first made it. Its reputation rests on its place, the Zhuge Liang sites at Longzhong that draw visitors to Xiangyang, and today it is presented as a mid-to-high-end regional speciality of the city.
